key_insight: Passively rotating flush-mounted discs produce only a modest net benefit: about 3% drag reduction relative to stationary discs, while housing and cover-plate interactions add drag penalties.
engineering_relevance: The study shows that passive rotating surfaces can alter turbulent boundary-layer skin friction, but the surrounding geometry must be carefully designed because small drag savings can be offset by roughness and secondary-flow effects.
method: Wind-tunnel experiments on turbulent boundary layers at friction Reynolds numbers Reτ = 880–1460
Thirty-two flush-mounted discs arranged in a staggered layout, half-covered by rigid plates to sustain passive rotation
Direct force measurements, PIV flow diagnostics, and the extended Elnahhas-Johnson skin-friction identity
evidence_signal: Direct force measurements and PIV indicate a 3% drag reduction from disc motion, with measured roughness and downwash effects explaining local changes in wall-normal transport.
watch_item: The reported drag benefit is small and depends on cavity, gap, and cover-plate effects, so implementation may not scale well without minimizing geometric losses.
paper_title: Turbulent boundary layers altered by passively rotating discs
